query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: The ability of near‐equiatomic multicomponent nanoparticles to preserve their structural and chemical integrity during catalytic (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric (473–1923 K) operation is governed by the extent and nature of local short‐range chemical ordering (SRO) within the nanoparticles. This SRO inhibits rapid atomic diffusion and phase segregation by creating local energy barriers that counteract high-temperature sintering and elemental rearrangement.
generation.material_initial_state: Homogeneous, near‐equiatomic high-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles produced by a solution-based (e.g., colloidal solvothermal) synthesis, exhibiting high configurational entropy and random chemical disorder.
generation.intervention: A controlled post-synthesis thermal annealing treatment at an intermediate temperature (e.g., ~600 K) under an inert or reducing atmosphere to promote a moderate degree of SRO without triggering full phase segregation, compared against as-synthesized (non-annealed) nanoparticles.
generation.conditions: Accelerated stability testing under catalytic conditions at 773–1173 K in a controlled reducing atmosphere and thermoelectric performance testing in the 473–1923 K range.
generation.structural_mediator: Local chemical ordering (SRO) as manifested by the formation of energetically favorable atomic motifs and reduced local lattice disorder.
generation.mechanism: The controlled development of SRO increases local energy barriers for atomic migration, thereby reducing atomic diffusion and suppressing phase separation or sintering that would otherwise compromise structural integrity and active surface composition at high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles that receive the intermediate annealing treatment (and hence exhibit enhanced SRO) will show less sintering, reduced phase segregation, and a more stable catalytic (and thermoelectric) performance under service conditions compared to the untreated baseline.
generation.baseline: As-synthesized HEA nanoparticles with a fully random distribution of constituent elements and no intentional SRO-promoting treatment.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to near-equiatomic single-phase solid-solution HEA nanoparticles operating under high-temperature conditions in inert or reducing atmospheres. Its applicability in strongly oxidizing environments or for non-equiatomic (or multiphase) systems remains to be tested.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative relationship between the degree of SRO and long-term stability is not precisely established, and the optimal balance between too little and too much ordering (which might impede catalytic activity) remains to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two batches of HEA nanoparticles using the same colloidal method. Subject one batch to a controlled thermal annealing at ~600 K under an inert atmosphere for a pre-defined duration to induce moderate SRO, while leaving the other batch untreated. Expose both batches to accelerated aging tests in a reducing atmosphere at 800–1100 K for extended durations. Characterize before and after aging using transmission electron microscopy (TEM), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) to assess phase integrity, particle size, and chemical homogeneity. Perform catalytic tests (e.g., ammonia decomposition) and thermoelectric measurements to compare performance retention.
measurements: TEM to measure particle morphology and sintering
XRD for phase identification and lattice strain
XPS for surface composition and chemical state analysis
Catalytic activity tests under controlled reaction conditions
Thermoelectric performance measurements over a range of temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed nanoparticles do not show a statistically significant improvement in structural and chemical stability (e.g., identical or worse particle coalescence, phase segregation, or catalytic/thermoelectric performance degradation) compared to the unannealed baseline, or if the induced SRO leads to an unexpected detriment (such as loss of catalytic active sites), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have attracted much attention in various fields with regard to applications as structural materials, biomaterials, supercapacitors, and catalysts., HEAs comprise mixtures of five or more metallic elements at near equiatomic ratios and form simple single solid-solution phases having lattice structures including face-centered cubic (fcc) and body-centered cubic (bcc)., The high configurational entropy of these alloys stabilizes the solid-solution phase such that this phase appears rather than an intermetallic phase or phase segregation., The severe lattice distortion in these materials that results from differences in the atomic sizes of the constituent elements also causes low atomic diffusivity. The unique synergistic effects resulting from combining multiple elements provide high specific strength, ductility, corrosion resistance, and thermal stability, such that HEAs are unique and fascinating materials. In recent years, many researchers have reported that HEA nanoparticles (NPs) having sizes on the nanometer scale (that is, in the range of 1 to 100 nm) show promise with regard to catalytic applications. Various techniques for the synthesis of such NPs

High-entropy oxides (HEOs) have aroused growing interest due to fundamental questions relating to their structure formation, phase stability, and the interplay between configurational disorder and physical and chemical properties. Introducing Fe(II) and Mn(II) into a rocksalt HEO is considered challenging, as theoretical analysis suggests that they are unstable in this structure under ambient conditions. Here, we develop a bottom-up method for synthesizing Mn- and Fe-containing rocksalt HEO (FeO-HEO). We present a comprehensive investigation of its crystal structure and the random cation-site occupancy. We show the improved structural robustness of this FeO-HEO and verify the viability of an oxygen sublattice as a buffer layer. Compositional analysis reveals the valence and spin state of the iron species. We further report the antiferromagnetic order of this FeO-HEO below the transition temperature ~218 K and predict the conditions of phase stability of Mn- and Fe-containing HEOs. Our results provide fresh insights into the design and property tailoring of emerging classes of HEOs.
